author: Chinua Achebe
introFa: کتاب «No Longer at Ease» نوشته Chinua Achebe یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح B2 است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.
readingTipsFa: پیش از مطالعه هر بخش از کتاب «No Longer at Ease»، نگاهی سریع به تیترها و ساختار آن بیندازید.
واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.
پس از پایان هر فصل، نکات کلیدی و آموخته‌های خود را مرور کرده و به زبان خود خلاصه کنید.

content: 6 Book Reviews Steven H. Gale. Chinua Achebe's No Longer at Ease: A Critical Commentary. New York: Monarch Press, I975. 94 pages. $1.25. Peter Mills. Notes on Chinua Achebe's No Longer at Ease. Nairobi: Heinemann Educational Books, I974. 31 pages. Two study guides on Achebe's No Longer at Ease have just appeared on the critical scene, almost within six months of each other. The word "crit- ical" is used qualifiedly, for these guides have shed little new light on the standard interpretation of No Longer at Ease. From the outset, one is struck by the dissimilarities in format of the two guides. This is explainable by two facts: editorial requirements and the divergence in approach, in these matters, by British and American writers. Peter Mills adheres to the British-oriented format popularized by the publishing house of James Brodie, Ltd., under the general editorship of Norman T. Carrington, and entitled Notes on Chosen English Texts. Steven Gale adheres to the American Study Guide format made popular by Monarch Press and Cliff Notes. The two study guides under review here share the strengths and weaknesses of their models. For example, British-oriented study guides usually end with "Context Questions" while providing no bibliographies and avoiding documentation altogether. The American-oriented study guides, on the other hand, insist on "Comment" at every turn, to explain difficult phrases, and to enlarge on background material. Invariably, study guides by American writers end in extensive bibliographies and well-documented pronouncements. In general, British- oriented study guides are slim volumes (Mills's guide is only thirty-one pages long), while American study-guide writers tend to thicker volumes (c.f. Gale's ninety-four pages). With differing emphases and at different lengths, the two writers tell essentially the same story. From the onset, Peter Mills assumes a higher level of literary consciousness on the part of his readers, while Steven Gale condescends to his readers, assuming he is either writing for a fairly naive audience or preaching to literary morons. Hence, Gale's unnecessary, often annoying explication (in length passages) of words, some of which he introduces in his own commentary, like Protagonist, Flashback, Plot, Tragedy, Suspense, and so on. It seems that in his effort to fill editorial "slots" according to the Monarch Notes format, Gale was forced into ex- plicating terms in verbiage disproportionate to the relevance of these words to the business at hand. Peter Mills's analysis covers a lot of ground in a short compass and provides a sort of critical balance by pointing out weaknesses in the con- struction of No Longer at Ease: irrelevant passages and obtrusive social commentary. BOOK REVIEWS 117 Economics) as a man who "manages to live at ease" in the novel because he is less rigid in his moral principles than the idealistic young man, Obi, who is "no longer at ease" because "he cannot live a life of compromise." On the other hand, Steven Gale's analysis suffers from a verbosity that is unparalleled in similar study guides. His introduction (rather, a series of introductions) is an overkill. The editor's Note emphasizes the fact that Steven Gale researched and wrote his guide while he was a resident scholar in Africa, and one gets the impression (especially when the author feels compelled to go back to I44I in order to bring his readers up to date with Africa's early contact with Europeans and with the origin of the slave trade so we can read and understand No Longer at Ease) that he is using his study guide as a partial dumping ground for the fruits of his research. Historical facts such as Indirect Rule in Nigeria, on which Gale dwells, are matters too peripheral to the immediate object in hand. But by the irony of things, Gale's overkill is the source of his strength when he focuses on Achebe and on No Longer at Ease. With all his ver- bosity, he covers a lot of ground and his research is as complete as anyone would wish. His biography of Chinua Achebe is up-to-date and complete and he avails himself of every opportunity to cite Achebe's pronounce- ments in interviews and other publications, in order to substantiate his own insights. And one other plus in Gale's work is the completeness of his documentation: the bibliographical data and wide-ranging references are perfection. On the contrary, Peter Mills's analysis, although to the point, suffers from inadequate research and from a reluctance to cite his sources. He dispatches "Achebe's Life" in three short paragraphs, and when he dis- cusses the main theme of the novel (which, to him, is "Corruption"), he does not seem to take into account the social complexities of the novel, nor does he plumb the dilemmas confronting Obi. Judging from his bib- liographical entry, Peter Mills had read only two critical works on Achebe: G. D. Killam and Eustace Palmer. No one expects study guides to break fresh critical ground, and one is neither surprised nor really disappointed that the analyses by Mills and Gale, taken together, never go beyond G. D. Killam's flatfooted com- mentary in The Novels of Chinua Achebe (New York: Africana Publish- ing Corporation, I969). To get Killam's entire critical package on No Longer at Ease, one must read both study guides. Mills takes "corruption" as the central theme of No Longer at Ease-something very adequately covered by Killam. Gale, on the other hand, takes his cue from Killam's statement that "No Longer at Ease is a structure of 'ambiguities' " be- cause "irony is the characteristic mode of the novel," and somehow blows life into it. 6 Book Reviews Steven H. Gale. Chinua Achebe's No Longer at Ease: A Critical Commentary. New York: Monarch Press, I975. 94 pages. $1.25. Peter Mills. Notes on Chinua Achebe's No Longer at Ease. Nairobi: Heinemann Educational Books, I974. 31 pages. Two study guides on Achebe's No Longer at Ease have just appeared on the critical scene, almost within six months of each other. The word "crit- ical" is used qualifiedly, for these guides have shed little new light on the standard interpretation of No Longer at Ease. From the outset, one is struck by the dissimilarities in format of the two guides. This is explainable by two facts: editorial requirements and the divergence in approach, in these matters, by British and American writers. Peter Mills adheres to the British-oriented format popularized by the publishing house of James Brodie, Ltd., under the general editorship of Norman T. Carrington, and entitled Notes on Chosen English Texts. Steven Gale adheres to the American Study Guide format made popular by Monarch Press and Cliff Notes. The two study guides under review here share the strengths and weaknesses of their models. For example, British-oriented study guides usually end with "Context Questions" while providing no bibliographies and avoiding documentation altogether. The American-oriented study guides, on the other hand, insist on "Comment" at every turn, to explain difficult phrases, and to enlarge on background material. Invariably, study guides by American writers end in extensive bibliographies and well-documented pronouncements. In general, British- oriented study guides are slim volumes (Mills's guide is only thirty-one pages long), while American study-guide writers tend to thicker volumes (c.f. Gale's ninety-four pages). With differing emphases and at different lengths, the two writers tell essentially the same story. From the onset, Peter Mills assumes a higher level of literary consciousness on the part of his readers, while Steven Gale condescends to his readers, assuming he is either writing for a fairly naive audience or preaching to literary morons. Hence, Gale's unnecessary, often annoying explication (in length passages) of words, some of which he introduces in his own commentary, like Protagonist, Flashback, Plot, Tragedy, Suspense, and so on. It seems that in his effort to fill editorial "slots" according to the Monarch Notes format, Gale was forced into ex- plicating terms in verbiage disproportionate to the relevance of these words to the business at hand. Peter Mills's analysis covers a lot of ground in a short compass and provides a sort of critical balance by pointing out weaknesses in the con- struction of No Longer at Ease: irrelevant passages and obtrusive social commentary. BOOK REVIEWS 117 Economics) as a man who "manages to live at ease" in the novel because he is less rigid in his moral principles than the idealistic young man, Obi, who is "no longer at ease" because "he cannot live a life of compromise." On the other hand, Steven Gale's analysis suffers from a verbosity that is unparalleled in similar study guides. His introduction (rather, a series of introductions) is an overkill. The editor's Note emphasizes the fact that Steven Gale researched and wrote his guide while he was a resident scholar in Africa, and one gets the impression (especially when the author feels compelled to go back to I44I in order to bring his readers up to date with Africa's early contact with Europeans and with the origin of the slave trade so we can read and understand No Longer at Ease) that he is using his study guide as a partial dumping ground for the fruits of his research. Historical facts such as Indirect Rule in Nigeria, on which Gale dwells, are matters too peripheral to the immediate object in hand. But by the irony of things, Gale's overkill is the source of his strength when he focuses on Achebe and on No Longer at Ease. With all his ver- bosity, he covers a lot of ground and his research is as complete as anyone would wish. His biography of Chinua Achebe is up-to-date and complete and he avails himself of every opportunity to cite Achebe's pronounce- ments in interviews and other publications, in order to substantiate his own insights. And one other plus in Gale's work is the completeness of his documentation: the bibliographical data and wide-ranging references are perfection. On the contrary, Peter Mills's analysis, although to the point, suffers from inadequate research and from a reluctance to cite his sources. He dispatches "Achebe's Life" in three short paragraphs, and when he dis- cusses the main theme of the novel (which, to him, is "Corruption"), he does not seem to take into account the social complexities of the novel, nor does he plumb the dilemmas confronting Obi. Judging from his bib- liographical entry, Peter Mills had read only two critical works on Achebe: G. D. Killam and Eustace Palmer. No one expects study guides to break fresh critical ground, and one is neither surprised nor really disappointed that the analyses by Mills and Gale, taken together, never go beyond G. D. Killam's flatfooted com- mentary in The Novels of Chinua Achebe (New York: Africana Publish- ing Corporation, I969). To get Killam's entire critical package on No Longer at Ease, one must read both study guides. Mills takes "corruption" as the central theme of No Longer at Ease-something very adequately covered by Killam. Gale, on the other hand, takes his cue from Killam's statement that "No Longer at Ease is a structure of 'ambiguities' " be- cause "irony is the characteristic mode of the novel," and somehow blows life into it. Besides echoing Killam's view that the novel is structured on a skein of ironies and ambiguities, Gale adds that there are actually two plots in the novel: the corruption plot and the love plot, which provide the two cimaxes in the novel. He also comments on Achebe's use of language as a technical device so that three strands of language are woven unobtrusively throughout the novel: standard English, been-to English, and pidgin English. Anyone desperate enough to want a study guide to understand Achebe's No Longer at Ease has both my sympathy and my advice: try Gale's Chinua Achebe's No Longer at Ease: A Critical Commentary first, for what it is worth. For the most part, academics ignore "study guides," thinking that a solid meal of the original text along with some good teaching will always be more appetizing than the predigested pabulum of a study guide. While the teacher can afford to think in terms of the intrinsic value of a good piece of literature, the student is faced with the immediate problem of passing an exam. The publication of study guides has become a flourishing busi- ness, showing that for many students such guides are second only to coffee in resolving the problem of "getting over" a literature exam. To be pom- pous and moral and argue that study guides discourage critical thinking and encourage students to think in terms of the interpretation instead of an interpretation is all beside the point. If critics did not ignore the study guide, they might see that it has potential as a useful critical and peda- gogical tool. James Gibbs's Study Aid to "Kongi's Harvest" is a fine ex- ample of what a study guide can be. (See my review, RAL, 5 CI974}, 259-62.) Moreover, the study guide is much less a cause of poor critical thinking than it is a symptom. The phenomenon of the study guide is par- tially the result of the pressures that exams put on students and partially the result of the critic's avoidance of any responsibility for writing ma- terial accessible and useful to the undergraduate. Both Nigel Brown's Notes on Wole Soyinka's Kongi's Harvest and Biodun Onibonoje's The Lion and the Jewel: Notes, Q/A are so bad they would hardly warrant the ink and paper of even a short review, but they do offer examples of what has given the study guide its reputation: poor writing, misinformation, and a dreary lack of imagination. own in examining the structure of the novel.
